title: Best Street Food in Bangkok
description: Bangkok street food the critics keep coming back to: Jay Fai's crab omelette, Thipsamai's pad thai, oyster omelette and Yaowarat after dark. Sources cited.
text: Bangkok might be the world's greatest street food city, and the critics agree on a handful of places that are worth the queue. 1. Raan Jay Fai: crab omelette and drunken noodles Chef Jay Fai cooks over charcoal in her trademark ski goggles. Her shop at 327 Maha Chai Road holds one Michelin star, retained in the 2026 Thailand guide, and featured in Netflix's Street Food: Asia . Michelin singles out the crispy crab omelette and the yellow-curry prawns. It's open Wednesday to Saturday only. Expect a long queue and bring cash. 2. Thipsamai: pad thai A Maha Chai Road institution, trading as Thipsamai since 1966. It's best known for its signature pad thai with prawn oil, wrapped in a thin egg skin. It's often called "Michelin", but it isn't on the current 2026 Bib Gourmand list. 3. Yaowarat (Chinatown) after dark When the sun sets, Yaowarat Road fills with stalls. Guides consistently recommend it for grazing: seafood, noodles, toasted buns and sweets, all within a few blocks. 4. Nai Mong Hoi Tod: oyster omelette A small shop on Soi Phlap Phla Chai in Chinatown, on Michelin's 2026 Bib Gourmand list. It's known for crispy oyster omelette (hoi tod) and mussel omelette. Good to know Bring cash, go early or late to dodge peak queues, and check opening days, since many stalls close one day a week.

title: Ramen 101: Shoyu, Shio, Miso & Tonkotsu Explained
description: Shoyu, shio, miso or tonkotsu? What each ramen style means, where it comes from (Tokyo, Hakodate, Sapporo, Fukuoka) and which bowl to order first in Japan.
text: Walk into a ramen shop in Japan and the menu (or the ticket machine) will usually sort bowls by flavour: shoyu, shio, miso, tonkotsu. Here's what each one means, where it comes from, and why the four aren't quite the same kind of category. Photo: Douglas Paul Perkins / Wikimedia Commons (CC0). Stock photo, not from our trip. First, the five parts of a bowl Ramen is usually described as five components: tare (the concentrated seasoning at the bottom of the bowl), aroma oil , broth , noodles and toppings . The noodles are chūkamen, wheat noodles made with kansui, an alkaline mineral water that gives them their yellow colour and springy bite. Broths are either chintan (clear, skimmed and gently simmered) or paitan (boiled hard until bones emulsify into a cloudy, creamy soup). 1. Shoyu: the Tokyo classic Shoyu means soy sauce. The tare adds salt and umami, and the broth is usually clear. Tokyo-style ramen is the archetype: a soy-seasoned chicken broth, often with a touch of dashi, and slightly thin, curly noodles, topped with chāshū pork, menma (fermented bamboo shoots), spring onion and nori. 2. Shio: the lightest and oldest Shio means salt, and it's generally considered the oldest of the four. The tare is built from salt plus umami ingredients like kombu and niboshi (dried sardines), so the soup stays pale and clear. Hakodate in Hokkaido is the city most associated with shio ramen. 3. Miso: Sapporo's winter bowl Miso ramen was developed in Sapporo and reached national prominence around 1965. Miso is blended into the broth, giving a thick, nutty, slightly sweet soup that can take bold toppings. In Sapporo that often means sweetcorn, butter, bean sprouts, minced pork and garlic, with thick, curly, chewy noodles. 4. Tonkotsu: Kyushu's creamy pork-bone broth Tonkotsu means pork bone (not to be confused with tonkatsu, the breaded cutlet). It's a paitan broth: bones boiled at high heat for hours until the soup turns milky. Hakata ramen from Fukuoka is the best-known version, served with thin, straight noodles and self-serve toppings like pickled ginger, sesame and spicy mustard greens. Many shops offer kaedama , a noodle refill dropped into your leftover soup. Why the categories overlap Strictly speaking, shoyu, shio and miso are seasonings (tares), while tonkotsu is a type of broth. That's why you'll see mash-ups everywhere, like Yokohama's iekei ramen, a soy-seasoned pork broth often called tonkotsu-shoyu. Which style is your go-to? Tell us on Instagram. Cheat-sheet - Want light? Shio. - Want classic? Shoyu. - Cold day, big appetite? Miso. - Rich and creamy? Tonkotsu. Where to learn more The Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum, open since 1994, has exhibits on ramen history and a basement food court with branches of well-known shops from across Japan. Heading to Tokyo? Our Tokyo neighbourhood guide lists the areas known for ramen.

title: Where to Eat in Lisbon
description: Where to eat in Lisbon: pastéis de nata in Belém, garlic prawns at Cervejaria Ramiro, Time Out Market and petiscos in Chiado. A researched guide, sources cited.
text: Lisbon rewards an appetite: seafood, slow-cooked petiscos, and a pastry culture that's worth crossing town for. 1. Pastéis de Belém: the original custard tart Baking since 1837 to a closely guarded recipe at Rua de Belém 84–92, near the Jerónimos Monastery, this bakery is the name food writers reach for when it comes to pastéis de nata. Sprinkle with cinnamon and sugar, and eat them warm. 2. Cervejaria Ramiro: seafood feast A beer hall famous for garlic prawns, clams and its prego (steak sandwich) for dessert, as seen in the Lisbon episode of Anthony Bourdain's No Reservations (2012). Queues are part of the experience. 3. Time Out Market (Mercado da Ribeira) Opened in 2014 inside the Mercado da Ribeira in Cais do Sodré, this food hall gathers stalls from well-known Lisbon chefs under one roof. It's a great way to sample lots in one go. 4. Taberna da Rua das Flores A small Chiado tavern serving a daily-changing menu of Portuguese petiscos, at Rua das Flores 103. No reservations: a door waitlist starts once it's full (usually around 6 pm), and it's closed on Sundays. Some reviewers report it's cash only, so bring some. Good to know Lunch is often better value than dinner, and many traditional places close on Sundays.

title: Where to Eat in Tokyo: A First-Timer's Neighbourhood Guide
description: Where to eat in Tokyo on a first trip: Tsukiji breakfasts, Ameyoko snacks, Shinjuku's Omoide Yokocho, ramen areas and konbini, one neighbourhood at a time.
text: Tokyo is the easiest big city in the world to eat well in and the hardest to choose in. Wikipedia's ramen entry alone puts the city at around 5,000 ramen shops, and that's before sushi counters, yakitori alleys and basement food halls. The trick for a first visit isn't finding a good meal; it's picking a few neighbourhoods and letting each one do what it does best. 1. Tsukiji Outer Market: breakfast seafood and kitchen shops The famous wholesale fish market moved to Toyosu in October 2018, but the outer market in Tsukiji, between the Sumida River and Ginza, stayed put. It's a tangle of retail stalls, sushi restaurants, grocers and knife and kitchen-tool shops. Go early: historically most outer-market shops wound down by early afternoon, so treat it as a breakfast-and-brunch neighbourhood. Graze on grilled seafood, tamagoyaki (sweet rolled omelette) and a sushi set, then browse the kitchenware. 2. Ueno and Ameyoko: a street market by the tracks Ameya-Yokochō, or Ameyoko, runs alongside the JR Yamanote Line from Ueno Station towards Okachimachi, with more than 250 shops selling everything from dried fish and candy to clothes. Its name may come from the candy shops (ame-ya) of the post-war years. It's a stand-up, snack-as-you-go neighbourhood: fruit on sticks, seafood stands and cheap counters under the railway arches. 3. Shinjuku: memory lane and a basement food hall Northwest of Shinjuku Station, Omoide Yokocho ("memory lane") is a small network of alleys along the tracks packed with tiny eateries serving yakitori, kushiyaki, ramen and soba. Many are just a counter and a few stools, and most open from around 5 pm. For the daytime version of Tokyo food culture, head to a depachika, the department-store food basement: Isetan's Shinjuku flagship, Takashimaya and Keio all have food departments below ground. Think bento, wagashi (Japanese sweets), pickles and immaculate fruit. 4. Ramen neighbourhoods: Ikebukuro, Ogikubo and Ebisu Tokyo-style ramen is a soy-seasoned chicken broth with slightly thin, curly noodles, often with a touch of dashi. Ikebukuro, Ogikubo and Ebisu are often named as Tokyo's ramen areas. Most counters use a ticket machine: you pay first, hand over the ticket and sit down. New to the styles? Read our Ramen 101 before you go. 5. Asakusa: where Tokyo ramen began Ramen historians trace the first specialised ramen shop, Rairaiken, to Asakusa in 1910. The original closed in 1976, and Wikipedia reports a descendant of the founder reopened it in Asakusa in 2026, which makes Asakusa a fitting stop for noodle history fans. Pair it with the old-Tokyo snack stalls around the temple district. 6. Konbini: the 24-hour safety net Japan's convenience stores (7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart) are a food stop in their own right: onigiri, fried chicken, and the much-photographed egg sando. They're perfect for a cheap breakfast or a late-night bite on the way back to your hotel. What's your favourite konbini snack? Tell us on Instagram. From our trip, Oct 2024 Our own photos from Tokyo. Captions describe what is in each photo; the guide above remains a researched guide. Good to know - Pay first: ticket machines are common at ramen and casual counters. - Small places, small groups: alley bars and counters often seat fewer than ten people. - Timing: markets are for mornings; yokocho alleys come alive after dark. - Watch for touts in Kabukicho: japan-guide warns about exorbitant cover charges at tout-run bars.

title: Disclosure
description: How Plates Around the World makes money, including affiliate links, gifts, and paid partnerships.
text: Disclosure: how we make money Plates Around the World is a small, independent food publication. We keep it free to read in a few honest ways, and we'll always tell you which one is in play. Affiliate links. Some pages link to products on shops such as Amazon.in, Flipkart and other retailers, through affiliate programmes and networks (for example EarnKaro and Cuelinks). If you buy through one of these links, we may earn a small commission. It costs you nothing extra. Pages with affiliate links carry an "Affiliate" note before the first link. We only list gear and ingredients we actually use, or clearly say when we haven't tried something. Gifts, hosted meals and collaborations. Sometimes a brand sends us a product, or a restaurant hosts our meal. When that happens, the post is labelled "Free gift" or "Collaboration" at the top and says exactly what we received. Our opinions stay our own, and nobody gets to approve what we write. Paid partnerships. Paid content is labelled "Ad" or "Sponsored" at the top, and uses the platform's paid-partnership tag on social media. First-hand vs researched. Separately from all this, every guide says whether we ate there ourselves ("First-hand visit") or researched it ("Researched guide"). See How we research. AI. We don't use AI-generated images to show a partner's product or a restaurant's food. If an image in a post is AI-generated, we label it. We follow the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) guidelines for influencer advertising. Questions? Email plates.arounddtheworld@gmail.com. Last updated: 22 Oct 2026.

title: Butter Chicken (Murgh Makhani) at Home
description: Butter chicken (murgh makhani) at home: charred yoghurt-marinated chicken in a silky tomato, butter and cream sauce, and the court case over who invented it.
text: Butter chicken comes from Delhi's Punjabi restaurant kitchens, and who invented it is literally a court case. Moti Mahal credits its founder Kundan Lal Gujral, while the Daryaganj chain says his partner Kundan Lal Jaggi created it. The Delhi High Court is hearing the dispute. Our version keeps the char and the silky sauce. Serves 4. Ingredients Marinade - 700 g boneless chicken thighs, in chunks - 200 g thick yoghurt - 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste - 1½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder - 1 tsp garam masala - 1 tsp salt, juice of ½ lemon Sauce - 3 tbsp butter + 1 tbsp oil - 1 onion, finely chopped (optional) - 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste - 400 g tomato purée - 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp garam masala - 1 tbsp kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) - 1 tsp sugar or honey - 120 ml double cream - Salt to taste; coriander to garnish Method 1. Marinate. Mix the marinade ingredients with the chicken and rest it for at least 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge. 2. Char. Grill, air-fry or sear the chicken in a very hot pan until charred at the edges and just cooked. Set aside. 3. Build the sauce. Melt the butter with the oil, soften the onion for 6–8 min, then add the ginger-garlic paste for 1 min. 4. Simmer. Add the tomato purée, chilli and garam masala. Cook for 10–12 min until it thickens and the butter separates at the edges. Blend smooth if you like. 5. Finish. Stir in the chicken, the crushed kasuri methi, sugar and cream. Simmer for 5 min and season. 6. Serve with naan or jeera rice, a knob of butter and some coriander.
